newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein fails in protest over parliament ban.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein fails in protest over parliament ban.

text.p: Leaders of the IRA's political wing who won seats in Britain's May 1 election failed during a visit to parliament on Monday to overturn a ruling barring their use of offices there unless they swear allegiance to Queen Elizabeth.

Sinn Fein party leader Gerry Adams and chief negotiator Martin McGuinness had a nice long lunch at parliament, strolled at length on the House of Commons terrace and were given a two-day security pass to roam the building.
But they did not achieve the main purpose of the high-profile visit: remove a ruling that prohibits them from using the facilities of parliament without a British oath of allegiance.
Sinn Fein officials said a second round of meetings with House of Commons authorities had been cordial but fruitless and the party would now consider what legal avenues were open to it.
As he left parliament, Adams said he would not give up.

"I am a political leader with a political mandate. I live in Ireland. I want to see an end to the British occupation of my country... We will continue with that until we succeed. We will be coming back here," he said.

Commons speaker Betty Boothroyd last week ruled that Adams and McGuinness could not use parliamentary offices or facilities unless they joined other MPs in swearing allegiance to the queen before taking their seats.

Adams and McGuinness, who advocate a united Ireland, refuse to swear allegiance to the crown because they do not recognise British sovereignty over Northern Ireland, where the majority of the population is Protestant and loyal to London.

The two passed up an opportunity to make a symbolic speech from the bar of the House -- a white line marking the formal entrance to the Commons chamber -- but appeared on several occasions before the cameras to make their case.

Adams complained that Boothroyd's ban, which will take effect late on Tuesday, was unilateral and arbitrary and had denied a democratic right to voters in the two Northern Ireland constituencies that elected him and McGuinness.

Imposing curbs on Sinn Fein would also send a negative signal just when new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair is trying to give new momentum to talks about a political settlement in Northern Ireland, Adams added.
"We are all of us at a very defining juncture in the relationships of the peoples of these two islands," he said.
The presence of Sinn Fein at Westminster has enraged many, who say they cannot be distinguished from Irish Republican Army guerrillas.

A republican splinter group, the INLA, blew up British MP Airey Neave in 1979 as he left parliament's underground car park. McGuinness had a heated exchange in the MPs' lobby with Conservative MP Nigel Evans, who told him: "We can work together but not by bombs or bullets."
After receiving their photo-passes, the Sinn Fein leaders lingered over a haddock lunch before strolling up and down on the terrace overlooking the River Thames.
They were waiting for a television crew to take shots from nearby Westminster bridge, but building work prevented the camera crew from making the rendezvous.
After half an hour they gave up waiting. "It's the most restful period we have had for 25 years," Adams smiled.
McGuinness said Sinn Fein would take up this week or next an offer made last Friday by Blair to ease a ban on official contacts to help find a settlement to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict.
Britain's previous Conservative government banned contacts with Sinn Fein after the IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.
